reference.source: Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle
clinicalPearls: Metatarsalgia is a symptom of pain under the metatarsal heads from forefoot overload rather than a single diagnosis, so the underlying cause must be sought
Pain is typically felt on the plantar aspect of the forefoot, worse on weight bearing and in hard or high-heeled shoes, and often accompanied by plantar callosities under the affected heads
Mechanical contributors include a tight gastrocnemius, cavus or splayed forefoot, hallux disorders that transfer load laterally, and lesser-toe deformities that plantarflex the metatarsal heads
Transfer metatarsalgia describes overload of neighbouring metatarsals when one ray is short, elevated, or has been altered by hallux surgery
Distinguish diffuse mechanical metatarsalgia from focal causes such as interdigital neuroma, plantar plate tear, Freiberg's infraction, stress fracture, and sesamoid pathology
Careful palpation localises tenderness to the metatarsal head, the intermetatarsal space, or the metatarsophalangeal joint, guiding the differential
Weight-bearing radiographs assess metatarsal length and alignment, while ultrasound or MRI evaluates soft-tissue and bony causes
Management is directed at the cause and includes metatarsal offloading orthoses and bars, cushioned footwear, calf stretching, activity modification, and correction of contributing deformity
reference.pathophysiology: Metatarsalgia arises when load beneath the lesser metatarsal heads exceeds what the forefoot soft tissues can tolerate, causing pain, inflammation, and protective callosity. Normal forefoot loading depends on even metatarsal length and alignment, a mobile first ray that shares weight, an adequate plantar fat pad, and balanced toe function. Disturbance of any of these concentrates pressure: a tight gastrocnemius increases forefoot load throughout stance, hallux valgus or hallux rigidus shifts weight laterally, lesser-toe clawing or hammering plantarflexes the metatarsal heads, and a long or plantarflexed metatarsal bears excess load. Distal migration or atrophy of the protective plantar fat pad, common with age, removes cushioning. When one ray is shortened, elevated, or surgically altered, adjacent rays absorb the redistributed force, producing transfer metatarsalgia. The result is localised or diffuse plantar forefoot pain that reflects the specific mechanical derangement.
additionalDifferentials: Plantar plate tear or metatarsophalangeal joint instability
Freiberg's infraction of a metatarsal head
Inflammatory arthritis of the metatarsophalangeal joints
Plantar fibroma or other soft-tissue mass
additionalInvestigations: Standing clinical examination with palpation of metatarsal heads, intermetatarsal spaces, and joints
Assessment of gastrocnemius tightness, forefoot alignment, and associated hallux and lesser-toe deformity
Weight-bearing foot radiographs to assess metatarsal length, alignment, and joint change
Ultrasound to evaluate for interdigital neuroma or plantar plate pathology
MRI where stress fracture, Freiberg's infraction, or occult soft-tissue lesion is suspected
Pedobarography to map the distribution of forefoot loading
Inflammatory markers and serology if inflammatory arthropathy is considered
redFlags: Focal bony tenderness and swelling suggesting a metatarsal stress fracture, particularly with a change in activity
Rest or night pain, or a destructive lesion on imaging, suggesting infection or tumour
Systemic or polyarticular features indicating inflammatory arthritis
Plantar ulceration or sensory loss in a neuropathic or diabetic foot
Progressive lesser-toe deformity with instability indicating an evolving plantar plate tear
reference.prognosis: Most mechanical metatarsalgia responds well to identifying and correcting the underlying cause with footwear, orthoses, calf stretching, and activity modification. Outcomes are good when contributing deformity is addressed, whereas symptoms persist or recur if the mechanical driver, such as a tight gastrocnemius or uncorrected toe deformity, is overlooked. Focal causes have their own prognosis and may require targeted intervention.
pitfalls: Treating metatarsalgia as a diagnosis rather than identifying the specific underlying cause
Missing a focal cause such as stress fracture, neuroma, or plantar plate tear behind diffuse forefoot pain
Overlooking a tight gastrocnemius that maintains forefoot overload
Failing to recognise transfer metatarsalgia following hallux surgery or with a short or elevated ray
Neglecting fat pad atrophy and footwear factors in older patients
references: Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle
management: Identify and correct the underlying mechanical driver rather than treating pain alone, as metatarsalgia is a symptom of forefoot overload
Modify footwear to cushioned, wide, low-heeled shoes with a stiff or rocker sole to reduce forefoot pressure
Prescribe orthoses with metatarsal pads, domes, or bars and custom insoles to offload the affected metatarsal heads
Advise gastrocnemius and calf stretching, activity modification, weight optimisation, and callus care
Target specific focal causes appropriately, such as interdigital neuroma, plantar plate tear, Freiberg's infraction, or stress fracture
Consider corrective surgery such as metatarsal osteotomy or correction of hallux and lesser-toe deformity for refractory structural cases
Refer to podiatry or orthopaedics when symptoms persist despite conservative measures
